Front: Explain how the ClassLoader verification step prevents security breaches in Java.
Back: Verification parses bytecode instructions to verify stack state, type compatibility, and check access permissions before execution.
Extra: If a class file was modified by a malicious tool (e.g., bypass private fields), verification rejects it with a VerifyError instead of letting the JVM execute unsafe instructions.

Front: Why does Preparation step initialize static fields to default values rather than their declared values?
Back: Because value assignment is part of class execution, which is deferred to the Initialization phase.
Extra: This separates resource allocation from logic execution. E.g., public static int x = 42; gets value 0 in Preparation and 42 only during Initialization.

Front: How does JIT compilation optimize hot code via method inlining?
Back: It replaces a method call instruction with the actual body of the target method, eliminating stack frame overhead.
Extra: This is a major compiler optimization that removes call instruction latency and opens up further optimization paths like constant folding and dead code elimination.

Front: Explain how Escape Analysis allows the JIT compiler to optimize object allocations.
Back: It determines if an object's reference escapes the scope of the allocating thread or method.
Extra: If the object does not escape, the JVM can allocate it on the thread stack instead of the heap (scalar replacement), saving GC cleanup overhead entirely.

Front: Why are there two Survivor spaces (S0 and S1) instead of just one?
Back: To allow copying and evacuating active objects back and forth, leaving one space completely empty and the other contiguous.
Extra: If there were only one survivor space, GC would have to mark-and-sweep or compact in place, leading to heap memory fragmentation or expensive in-memory shifting.

Front: Explain the risk of premature promotion in JVM Garbage Collection.
Back: Short-lived objects are promoted to the Old Generation too early because Survivor spaces are full.
Extra: This causes the Old Generation to fill up rapidly, leading to frequent Major or Full GC cycles, which significantly degrades application throughput and latency.

Front: How does Shenandoah GC handle concurrent writes while an object is being relocated?
Back: It intercepts writes via a write barrier and uses Compare-And-Swap (CAS) to update the Brooks Pointer of the old object to point to the new copy before writing.
Extra: This ensures that any mutation is immediately written to the new to-space copy of the object rather than the stale from-space object, avoiding data loss.

Front: What performance overhead does Shenandoah's load barrier introduce?
Back: A tiny CPU cycle overhead on every object reference read because the barrier must dereference the Brooks Pointer.
Extra: Although there is a minor throughput cost (typically 2-5% decrease in overall speed), it is a trade-off for eliminating long Stop-The-World pause latency.

Front: Why should JVM memory flags -Xms and -Xmx be set to the same value in production?
Back: To prevent the JVM from continuously sizing and resizing the heap dynamically.
Extra: Heap resizing operations trigger Stop-The-World events and CPU spikes. Setting -Xms equal to -Xmx pre-allocates maximum memory at startup, improving latency stability.

Front: What is the danger of setting -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis to an aggressively low value (e.g., 5ms)?
Back: It forces the GC to run extremely frequently on very small regions, leading to severe throughput degradation.
Extra: The JVM spends all its CPU resources doing incremental GC work instead of executing application business logic, a state known as GC thrashing.

Front: Explain the difference between JVM standard options and experimental options.
Back: Standard options are stable and portable across vendors, while experimental options are vendor-specific and must be unlocked explicitly.
Extra: Standard flags do not change across versions easily, but experimental -XX flags can be added or deleted without any notice between minor JDK releases.

Front: How does the JVM ClassLoader ensure that core system classes (like java.lang.Object) are not overridden?
Back: By using the delegation model where class loading requests are delegated up to the Bootstrap ClassLoader first.
Extra: If a user writes a custom class named java.lang.Object, the Bootstrap ClassLoader loads the original system version first, preventing class spoofing security attacks.
